problem: Existing instruction-following navigation benchmarks (R2R, RxR, ObjNav, DDN) test semantic and multimodal understanding but do not systematically evaluate spatial perception and reasoning (floors, scale, viewpoint, ordering, structure). It is unclear how MLLMs and navigation models perform on such instructions.
motivation: Spatial-intelligence instructions are common in daily life (e.g., 'go to the top floor', 'walk 3 m then turn right 60°'). Static spatial benchmarks (VSI-Bench, MindCube) do not measure whether spatial perception turns into correct dynamic actions, so a dedicated navigation benchmark and a way to improve models are needed.
key_idea: Build NavSpace, a questionnaire-derived benchmark of 1,228 human-collected trajectory-instruction pairs in six spatial-intelligence categories, and improve a navigation LLM (SNav) by fine-tuning on automatically synthesized spatial instructions built from R2R and MP3D.
insight: Models that do well on static spatial benchmarks or on VLN (BEVBert, ETPNav, GPT-4o) fail on NavSpace, so spatial perception does not automatically become action. GPT-5 often answers spatial questions correctly yet issues inconsistent actions, and lightweight models rely on shallow semantic-to-action mapping. Removing individual synthetic data pipelines lowers average SR from 26.0 to 18.4-22.4, with the Spatial Relationship data removal hurting most, so targeted spatial data helps.
method: Benchmark construction: questionnaire (457 valid responses, 17 candidate types) picks six categories: Vertical Perception, Precise Movement, Viewpoint Shifting, Spatial Relationship, Environment State, Space Structure.
Trajectory collection: annotators teleoperate in Habitat 3.0 with HM3D scenes via a web platform, recording RGB, actions and coordinates.

Instruction annotation and validation: GPT-5 analyzes the trajectory and drafts instructions, humans write the final ones, and a different annotator must reach the goal (else re-annotate). Success radius is 1-3 m depending on category.

SNav architecture: SigLIP encoder + 2-layer MLP projector + Qwen2 LLM, initialized from LLaVA-Video 7B, and co-trained (CorrectNav-style) on action prediction, trajectory-to-instruction generation and general multimodal data recall.

Synthetic spatial data: Cross-floor (R2R trajectories with height change, GPT-5 detects stairs, HOV-SG floor labels, instructions restyled with floor numbers); Precise Movement (MP3D shortest paths merged into metric/angle descriptions and paraphrased by GPT-5); Environment State (if/otherwise templates from first/last frames); Spatial Relationship (regex selection of R2R instructions with ordinals and between/along/across).
Evaluation: Habitat with actions forward 0.25 m, turn ±30°, stop; metrics NE, OS, SR; 22 agents in 5 groups plus chance baselines.

setting.training_data: Navigation co-training (action prediction, instruction generation, general multimodal recall) following CorrectNav, plus synthesized spatial instructions from R2R and MP3D scenes (cross-floor, precise movement, environment state, spatial relationship); scale not stated
setting.action_space: low-level discrete: move forward 0.25 m, turn left 30°, turn right 30°, stop
setting.simulator: Habitat 3.0 (HM3D scenes for evaluation; MP3D/R2R for training data)

results: SNav reaches average SR 26.0 / OS 36.7 / NE 4.47 on NavSpace, beating NaVid (20.0), StreamVLN (19.2), GPT-5 (14.2) and Gemini 2.5 Pro (11.2). Open-source MLLMs stay below 10% SR, close to frequency chance (8.3). On a real quadruped SNav gets 32% versus NaVid 14% and NaVILA 6%.
limitations: Benchmark is simulation-only (HM3D), small (1,228 pairs), and absolute success is still low (26%).

The synthetic spatial data pipelines cover only four categories (none for Viewpoint Shifting or Space Structure); the Space Structure NE and Viewpoint Shifting results are not clearly better than NaVid.
The real-world test is small (10 trials per category) and excludes vertical perception.
